metadata.title: Synergistic effects of instruction and affect factors on high- and low-ability disparities in elementary students’ reading literacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 microdata for Grade 4 reading literacy from seven English- and Chinese-speaking education systems (Australia, United States, England, Northern Ireland, Hong Kong, Macao, Chinese Taipei). The analytic sample is restricted to students whose reading scores fall at or above the PIRLS advanced benchmark (high achievers) or below the intermediate benchmark (low achievers), and models are trained separately for the English-speaking and Chinese-speaking system groups. The manuscript does not report applying PIRLS sampling weights or replicate weights, and the ML pipeline is implemented in Python/scikit-learn, which typically does not natively incorporate complex survey weights. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as classification performance on the selected sample rather than as fully population-representative estimates across the complex PIRLS sampling design.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading literacy microdata. Restricted to English-speaking education systems where students’ reading subject test language (ITLANG) is English: United States, England, Northern Ireland, and Australia; and to Chinese-speaking systems: Hong Kong, Macao, and Chinese Taipei. Further restricted to a binary classification dataset by labeling students as high achievers if their reading score is at or above the advanced benchmark (>=625) and as low achievers if their reading score is below the intermediate benchmark (<475). Excluded invalid responses (e.g., outlier code '99' on Likert items) by treating them as missing, removed observations with a large proportion of missing values, and imputed remaining missing values using nearest-neighbor averaging before model training.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (English-speaking systems subset: AUS, USA, GBR-ENG, GBR-NIR)
main_findings.target_variable: High vs low reading achiever (binary; advanced >=625 vs intermediate <475)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Logistic regression — Testing Accuracy 84.07%, Precision 82.88%, Recall 88.02%, F-score 84.07%; Linear SVM — Testing Accuracy 86.59%, Precision 85.17%, Recall 90.33%, F-score 86.59%, AUC not reported; Decision Tree — Testing Accuracy 84.07%, Precision 84.67%, Recall 85.28%, F-score 84.07%; XGBoost — Testing Accuracy 88.19%, Precision 88.99%, Recall 88.60%, F-score 88.19%, AUC not reported. Best model: XGBoost (highest testing accuracy and F-score).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading data for English-speaking systems, the study leveraged reading self-concepts, reading attitudes, perceptions of instruction, and key instructional practices (e.g., inferences/generalizations and longer fiction with chapters) to classify high vs low achievers, finding that the combined instruction+affect factor set discriminated proficiency levels with strong performance and that affective constructs—especially reading self-concepts—were the predominant contributors. This indicates that strengthening students’ reading self-concepts alongside targeted comprehension-oriented instruction may be a high-leverage strategy for reducing high–low reading disparities, though the study is predictive (not causal) and does not report survey-weighted inference.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (Chinese-speaking systems subset: HKG, MAC, TWN)
main_findings.target_variable: High vs low reading achiever (binary; advanced >=625 vs intermediate <475)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Logistic regression — Testing Accuracy 83.76%, Precision 85.71%, Recall 88.76%, F-score 83.76%; Linear SVM — Testing Accuracy 85.24%, Precision 87.72%, Recall 88.76%, F-score 85.24%; Decision Tree — Testing Accuracy 82.10%, Precision 83.75%, Recall 88.46%, F-score 82.10%; XGBoost — Testing Accuracy 88.01%, Precision 89.34%, Recall 91.72%, F-score 88.01%, AUC not reported. Best model: XGBoost (highest testing accuracy and recall).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading data for Chinese-speaking systems, the study leveraged reading self-concepts, reading attitudes, perceptions of instruction, and selected instructional practices (e.g., same-ability grouping and comprehension-oriented activities) to classify high vs low achievers, finding that the combined instruction+affect factor set was sufficiently powerful to discriminate proficiency levels and that affective engagement—particularly reading self-concepts—again dominated the separation task. This indicates that classroom interventions aiming to build students’ confidence and positive reading self-beliefs, together with culturally aligned instructional routines, may help narrow the high–low reading gap, while causality cannot be inferred from the predictive ML classification and survey-weight handling is not reported.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading literacy for 9,748 students from seven English- and Chinese-speaking education systems, restricting the sample to binary high vs low achievers using PIRLS benchmarks (advanced ≥625 vs intermediate <475). It trains four supervised ML classifiers—logistic regression, linear SVM, decision tree, and XGBoost—separately for English-speaking and Chinese-speaking system groups, using a 80/20 train-test split with 5-fold cross-validation and grid search for tuning. Missing values from invalid Likert codes were imputed using nearest-neighbor averaging after removing cases with high missingness; features were normalized to [0,1] but left unscaled for tree-based models. Across both system groups, XGBoost achieved the best testing performance (English: Accuracy 88.19%, F-score 88.19%; Chinese: Accuracy 88.01%, Recall 91.72%). The most influential predictors were affective constructs—especially reading self-concepts—suggesting that improving students’ reading confidence and related beliefs may be central to reducing high–low disparities, though the approach is predictive (not causal) and does not report complex survey weighting.
